title: ABRAHAM’S CONCUBINES: THE WOMEN AND CHILDREN EVERYONE FORGETS AFTER SARAH
paragraphs: ABRAHAM’S CONCUBINES: THE WOMEN AND CHILDREN EVERYONE FORGETS AFTER SARAH

We remember Sarah. We remember Isaac. We remember the promise. But buried near the end of Abraham’s story is one uncomfortable sentence about other women, other sons, gifts placed into departing hands—and a family separation Scripture refuses to erase.
Most people think they know how Abraham’s story ends.
Sarah dies.
Isaac remains.
Abraham grows old.
The patriarch dies in faith.
Curtain closed.
Except the Bible does something strange before Abraham leaves the stage.
It opens another door.
And standing behind that door are people many Christians barely remember.
A woman named Keturah.
Six sons.
Grandsons.
Entire family lines.
And then one sentence that should make us stop reading so quickly:
“But unto the sons of the concubines, which Abraham had, Abraham gave gifts…”
Genesis 25:6.
Sons.
Concubines.
Plural.
Suddenly the ending of Abraham’s life feels more complicated than the version many of us remember from Sunday school.
Because Abraham’s household was not a polished family portrait.
It contained promise and pain.
Faith and human failure.
Miraculous intervention and complicated consequences.
A beloved wife named Sarah.
An Egyptian servant named Hagar.
A woman named Keturah.
Isaac, the covenant son.
Ishmael, the son Abraham loved but who was not the covenant heir.
Other sons whose names rarely survive in Christian memory.
And through all of it, a God whose redemptive purpose continued despite the tangled humanity of the people He called.
That matters.
Because perhaps you came to Jesus carrying a tangled story too.
Before going further, however, we need to be precise about what Scripture actually says.
Genesis 25 introduces Keturah with these words:
“Then again Abraham took a wife, and her name was Keturah.”
The Hebrew begins:
וַיֹּסֶף אַבְרָהָם וַיִּקַּח אִשָּׁה וּשְׁמָהּ קְטוּרָה
Vayyosef Avraham vayyiqqach ishah, ushemah Qeturah.
In straightforward sense: Abraham again took a woman as wife, and her name was Keturah.
The important word is אִשָּׁה — ishah.
Depending on context, it can mean “woman” or “wife.”
So Genesis 25:1 presents Keturah as Abraham’s wife.
But Scripture gives us another description.
First Chronicles 1:32 calls her:
קְטוּרָה פִּילֶגֶשׁ אַבְרָהָם
Keturah, Abraham’s pilegesh—his concubine.
That is not a contradiction that needs to be hidden.
It gives us a fuller picture of her status.

A concubine in the ancient world was not simply what modern readers might imagine when hearing words such as “mistress” or “affair.” She occupied a recognized but subordinate marital or household status and did not possess the same standing as the principal wife.
Keturah could therefore be described as a wife in Genesis while Chronicles identifies her more specifically as a concubine.
And then Genesis 25:6 makes the picture even more intriguing by speaking of Abraham’s “concubines” in the plural.
The Hebrew expression is:
בְּנֵי הַפִּילַגְשִׁים
benei happilagshim—
“the sons of the concubines.”
We should not pretend the Bible tells us more than it does.
It does not give us a neat list saying, “These were all Abraham’s concubines.”
Keturah is explicitly called his concubine in Chronicles.
Hagar requires slightly more careful language.
Genesis identifies Hagar as Sarah’s Egyptian servant, and Genesis 16:3 says Sarah gave Hagar to Abram:
לְאִשָּׁה
le’ishah—
“as a wife.”

That makes the story considerably more complex than reducing Hagar to merely Abraham’s secret lover. She entered a recognized relationship within the household through an ancient arrangement initiated by Sarah—an arrangement Scripture records without requiring us to treat the arrangement itself as God’s ideal.
And that distinction is crucial.
The Bible often tells us what happened without telling us to imitate everything that happened.
Abraham is a towering man of faith.
Abraham is also a man whose household reveals what happens when frightened human beings try to accomplish divine promises through human solutions.
God had promised Abraham descendants.
Years passed.
Sarah remained barren.
Waiting became painful.
Pain became pressure.
And pressure whispered the same dangerous sentence it still whispers today:
“Maybe God needs your help.”
So Hagar entered the story.
And Ishmael was born.
This is where we need to resist the temptation to turn Hagar into a villain.
She was an Egyptian servant caught inside decisions made by people with far more power than she possessed.
Genesis does not hide the ugliness that followed.
Pregnancy changed relationships.
Contempt appeared.
Sarah became harsh.
Hagar fled.
And then something astonishing happened.
God found her.
Not Abraham.
Not Sarah.
God.
An Egyptian servant woman running through the wilderness became the recipient of divine attention.
The angel of the LORD met her near a spring.
God heard her suffering.
God spoke about her unborn child.
God gave promises concerning Ishmael’s future.
And Hagar responded with one of Scripture’s most unforgettable declarations about God:
אַתָּה אֵל רֳאִי
Attah El Ro’i.
“You are a God who sees me.”
Think about that.
The woman human beings pushed toward the margins discovered that heaven had not lost sight of her.
Maybe that is where this story stops being ancient history.
Because some people reading this know exactly what it feels like to become collateral damage in somebody else’s choices.
Someone else made the decision.
You inherited the wound.
Someone else broke the covenant.
You lived with the consequences.
Someone else created the chaos.
You grew up inside it.
Someone else walked away.
You spent years wondering why you were apparently so easy to leave.
And somewhere inside you is a question you rarely say aloud:
“Does God see what happened to me?”
Hagar’s story answers from the wilderness.
Yes.
He sees.
But seeing Hagar does not mean God abandoned His covenant concerning Isaac.
That is another truth modern readers sometimes struggle to hold simultaneously.
God could care deeply for Ishmael while maintaining that Isaac was the covenant son through whom the particular covenant line would continue.
Grace toward one person did not require God to rewrite what He had promised concerning another.
Genesis eventually reaches Sarah’s death.
Then, almost unexpectedly, Keturah appears.
She bears Abraham six sons:
Zimran.
Jokshan.
Medan.
Midian.
Ishbak.
Shuah.
Then the genealogy expands again.
Jokshan fathers Sheba and Dedan.
Midian fathers Ephah, Epher, Hanoch, Abida, and Eldaah.
Names.
Names.
Names.
Names modern readers hurry past.
But God did not hurry past them.
Scripture recorded them.
That alone should humble us.
Because human beings measure significance by spotlight.
God does not.
We remember the person standing in the center of the photograph.
God remembers the people whose names barely fit into the caption.
We remember Isaac because the covenant narrative continues through Isaac.
But God remembered Ishmael.
God recorded Keturah.
God recorded Zimran.
God recorded Jokshan.
God recorded Medan.
God recorded Midian.
God recorded Ishbak.
God recorded Shuah.
People we forget remained visible to God.
Then comes the painful sentence.
Abraham gave everything he had to Isaac.
But to the sons of his concubines he gave gifts while he was still alive.
Then he sent them away from Isaac.
Eastward.
Away.
Imagine that moment without romanticizing it.
Possessions being gathered.
Gifts being distributed.
Camels being prepared.
Perhaps mothers watching.
Perhaps sons looking back.
Perhaps questions nobody knew how to answer.
Scripture does not tell us their private emotions, so we should not invent them as history.
But Scripture does tell us what happened.
Isaac received Abraham’s estate.
The other sons received gifts.
Then Abraham sent them eastward, away from Isaac.
Why?
The text places this separation alongside Isaac’s unique inheritance and covenant role.
Earlier God had already declared concerning Sarah:
“I will establish my covenant with him for an everlasting covenant, and with his seed after him.”
The covenant would continue through Isaac.
Not because Isaac was morally superior as a baby.
Not because Ishmael was worthless.
Not because Keturah’s children were invisible.
But because God had sovereignly chosen the covenant line through which His redemptive purpose would advance.
Isaac.
Then Jacob.
Then Israel.
Then Judah.
Then generation after generation...
until eventually another genealogy opens:
“The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham.”
There He is.
Jesus.
Suddenly Abraham’s complicated household belongs to a story much larger than Abraham.
The promise was moving somewhere.
Toward Christ.
This is why we must be careful when preaching Abraham.
The point is not that Abraham was flawless.
He was not.
The point is that God was faithful.
The Bible does not need Abraham to look perfect in order for God to look glorious.
That may be one of the most liberating truths in Scripture.
Because Christianity is not the announcement that God finally found enough impressive people to build His kingdom.
Christianity is the announcement that the holy God entered the wreckage of human history to redeem sinners through Jesus Christ.
Abraham believed God.
Abraham also experienced fear.
He obeyed magnificently at times.
He failed painfully at others.
His family experienced consequences.
Yet God remained faithful to His promise.
And eventually Jesus stepped into Abraham’s bloodline.
Not because every chapter before Him was clean.
But because grace had been moving through the mess all along.
That is the Gospel.
Jesus does not come from a Bible filled with airbrushed people.
He enters a biblical history filled with barrenness, jealousy, favoritism, sexual brokenness, family conflict, deception, exile, grief, failure, and sin.
Then at Calvary, the Son of God carries human sin upon Himself.
The scandal becomes the place where grace speaks.
The cross looked like defeat.
God made it the place of victory.
The condemned Christ became the risen Lord.
The grave received Him.
The grave could not keep Him.
And now everyone who comes to Christ in repentance and faith discovers something Abraham’s complicated household whispers from thousands of years ago:
Your history is real.
But your history does not have to become your master.
Maybe your family tree embarrasses you.
Maybe your father failed you.
Maybe your mother wounded you.
Maybe your marriage collapsed.
Maybe you were the one who caused the collapse.
Maybe there is a child you barely speak to anymore.
Maybe your past contains sexual sin.
Maybe you manipulated people.
Maybe you were manipulated.
Maybe you waited for God, became impatient, and created an Ishmael-sized consequence you cannot simply erase.
The Gospel does not ask you to rename darkness as light.
Repentance means bringing the truth into the presence of God.
No excuses.
No religious costume.
No carefully edited testimony.
Sin is sin.
Wounds are wounds.
Consequences can remain consequences.
But Jesus Christ is still Jesus Christ.
And grace is not God pretending your past never happened.
Grace is God refusing to let your past have the final word over everyone who belongs to Christ.
There is an enormous difference.
God did not delete Hagar from Genesis.
He met her.
God did not erase Ishmael.
He heard him.
God did not erase Keturah.
He recorded her.
God did not erase her sons.
He named them.
God did not rewrite Abraham’s story by pretending its painful chapters never existed.
He carried His promise through them.
And perhaps that is what someone reading this desperately needed tonight.
You keep asking God to erase the chapter.
Maybe redemption is not erasure.
Maybe redemption is Christ taking a chapter that should have ended in shame and making it testify to mercy.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by changing yesterday’s facts.
By changing what yesterday gets to mean for your eternity.
If you have been hiding something from God, stop running.
He already sees you.
If you have been excusing sin because someone else hurt you first, stop.
Their sin does not sanctify yours.
If you have been convinced you are beyond forgiveness, look at the cross again.
Christ did not shed symbolic blood for imaginary sinners.
He died for real sinners carrying real guilt.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Bring the secret into His light.
Come home.
And if this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to explain your entire story publicly.
Just comment, “Jesus, have mercy on me.”
If your faith has been exhausted and you are still trying to hold on, comment, “I’m still fighting.”
And if you have watched Jesus begin redeeming something in your life that once looked impossible to redeem, comment, “Christ is still healing me.”
Your testimony may become the sentence somebody else desperately needed to read tonight.
Not because sharing a Facebook article earns favor with God.
It does not.
We are saved by grace, not social-media activity.
But if biblical truth helped you, sharing it can place that truth in front of someone you may never realize was silently drowning.
Send it privately to the person whose family is breaking apart.
Not to purchase God’s favor.
Not to prove that you love Jesus.
Not because financial support makes anyone more spiritual.
The Gospel cannot be bought.
But ministry does require people willing to help carry it.
And there is something else we want believers to know.
Thousands.
Free.
Because not everyone can afford a shelf full of Christian books, but everyone should be encouraged to open Scripture, seek Christ, grow in truth, and become deeply rooted in the Gospel.
Leave asking something deeper about yourself.
Which chapter are you still hiding?
Which consequence have you mistaken for a life sentence?
Which wound has become your identity?
Which failure convinced you that Jesus could forgive everybody except you?
Abraham’s story did not end with Hagar running into the wilderness.
It did not end with Sarah’s grave.
It did not end with Keturah’s sons traveling east.
It did not even end inside the cave where Isaac and Ishmael together buried their father.
The promise kept moving.
Generation after generation.
Until Bethlehem.
Until a carpenter’s home.
Until Galilee.
Until blind eyes opened.
Until lepers were cleansed.
Until sinners sat at the table.
Until nails entered holy hands.
Until blood ran down a Roman cross.
Until a stone sealed a borrowed tomb.
Until Sunday morning.
That is where every story of biblical redemption ultimately points.
Not Abraham.
Jesus.
Not human faithfulness.
His faithfulness.
Not our ability to repair ourselves.
His power to save.
So if your family history looks more like Genesis than a Christian greeting card, you may be closer to understanding grace than you realize.
The Bible was never frightened by broken families.
Jesus entered one long human history filled with broken people to rescue broken people.
Bring Him the scandal.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the family secret.
Bring Him the consequence.
Bring Him the part of your story you wish nobody knew.
Then repent where you must repent.
Forgive where Christ calls you to forgive.
Seek reconciliation where reconciliation is righteous and possible.
Make restitution where repentance requires it.
And trust the Savior who carried sin and shame to the cross.
Because the forgotten women around Abraham’s household remind us of something we dare not forget:
God sees people standing outside the spotlight.
He hears cries from the wilderness.
He remembers names other people skip.
And His redemptive purpose is not defeated by the tangled histories of human beings.
So comment if you need prayer.
Share if someone in your world needs this truth.
Because somewhere tonight, another Hagar is convinced nobody sees her.
Another Ishmael feels pushed outside the promise.
Another family is living with consequences nobody posts about.
Another believer thinks one terrible chapter has destroyed the entire book.
And somebody needs to tell them:
The chapter that embarrasses you may be the very place where you finally discover how desperately you need the Savior who refuses to abandon repentant sinners to their shame.
